1:
Why a second letter was needed at all is Calvin's first question, and his answer governs the rest. Lest they should be wearied with it as though the first were sufficient, Peter says it was not written in vain, because they needed to be often stirred up; for the minds of the godly become dim and, as it were, contract rust when admonitions cease, and even men endued with learning grow drowsy unless roused by constant warnings. He grants that they had a sincere mind, freed from the pollutions of the preceding chapter, and yet says their minds were not on that account perfect. From this he draws the use of admonition in general: the sloth of the flesh smothers the truth once received unless the goads of warning come to its aid, so that it is not enough for men to be taught what they ought to be, but there is need of godly teachers to do the second part and impress the truth deeply on the memory. Henry finds the same tenderness in the manner rather than the argument, since the apostle writes the same thing in other words — it being safe for them, it should not be grievous to him — and calls them beloved, showing that ministers must be examples of love and affection as well as of life and conversation.

On the word rendered pure the two grammarians agree and give the derivation. Ellicott says it means literally separated, either by being sifted or by being held up to the light, and so unsullied, probably here untainted by sensuality; the word for mind means the faculty of moral reflection and moral understanding, and the two stand together in a passage of Plato. Robertson gives the doubtful etymology, sunlight and to judge by it, and notes that Plato used the adjective of ethical purity. Ellicott also reads the opening clause as evidence about the letter itself, since this already a second epistle implies no very long time since the first and much the same circle of readers; he denies that the first two chapters are one letter and this the beginning of another, and sets out how the last chapter answers the first, its opening recalling the earlier charge to stir them up and its close the earlier call to make their calling sure.

The commandment of the apostles raises the sharpest question, and it is a question about who wrote the letter. Ellicott holds that of us is beyond doubt a false reading and should be your apostles, and turns this into an argument for genuineness: a true apostle, having once stated his credentials, might well sink his own personality among his colleagues from humility toward readers who owed their Christianity mainly to others, whereas a writer personating an apostle would have insisted on his assumed authority here. Robertson agrees that your is correct, reports the view that Peter would not have spoken so of the twelve and that the forger here allows the mask to slip, and calls that a needless inference. Barnes, keeping the other reading, draws the opposite kind of conclusion, that no man would have used such language who did not regard himself and his fellow apostles as inspired and on a level with the prophets. On which commandment is meant, Ellicott answers that it is surely not the whole Christian law but either the charge to beware of false teachers or, more probably, to be ready for Christ's coming; Calvin calls it a metonymy, the commandment standing for the doctrine taught. Barnes explains why the prophets are appealed to at all, since when Peter wrote the canon of the New Testament was not complete and probably very little of it was known to these readers; and Clarke guesses at the particular prophecies, those of Enoch mentioned by Jude, of David, and of Daniel.
3:
Calvin says why the warning was needed: had impious men attacked them suddenly with scoffs of this kind they might have been shaken, so he wished them to know it beforehand and be prepared to oppose such men. He then states the rule he draws from it, that the more God offers himself by the gospel to the world the more audacious will ungodly men vomit forth the poison of their impiety; and he warns that nothing is more to be feared than a contest with scoffers, since it is the very extremity of evil when men treat the awful name of God with scoffs. Henry expects the same increase and explains it by the dispensation: it may seem strange that the New Testament covenant, being spiritual and therefore more agreeable to the nature of God than the Old, should be the thing ridiculed, but its spirituality and simplicity are directly contrary to the carnal mind of man, so that in the last days there will be a great improvement in the art and impudence of bantering serious godliness. Clarke traces the same conduct to its root: the gospel requires a holy heart and holy life, and they wish to follow their own lusts, so they labour to prove it untrue in order to be rid of its injunctions, and at last persuade themselves it is a forgery. Barnes narrows the class, since it scarcely required inspiration to foresee scoffers in general, they having abounded in every age; the apostle's eye is on a particular body of men whose reproaches would take a definite form.

On the wording the textual men agree and add something each. Clarke reports the addition found in almost every manuscript and version of note, that they shall come in mockery, since received into the text; Ellicott says the best authorities add in scoffing, intensifying by repetition; and Robertson calls it Peter's play on words, both terms coming from a verb meaning to trifle with and neither found elsewhere. On the last days, Calvin takes the Hebrew form, the extremity of the days, and understands the days of the gospel dispensation; Barnes insists the phrase does not imply the world was about to end, and that this period might be longer than all the previous ones; Clarke thinks it probably refers to the conclusion of the Jewish polity, then at hand.

The scoff itself divides them over who the fathers are. Ellicott sets out four answers — the ancestors of the human race, the patriarchs and prophets, the first generation of Christians, and each generation in relation to the next — and concludes that probably nothing more definite than our remote ancestors is meant. He then refutes the objection that the fathers are the first Christians, and that such a scoff would be impossible in the apostle's lifetime, by pointing to a passage which a writer at the close of the first century could already quote as Scripture, in which the double-minded say they heard these things in the times of their fathers also and have grown old and none of them has happened. Wesley and Gill take the plainer sense, that they do not even deign to name him, and that the demand is not where the promise stands written but what has become of it. Calvin looks past the wording to what is at stake: it was a dangerous scoff, for Satan aims directly at the throat of the Church when he destroys faith in the coming of Christ, since all religion is wholly subverted unless faith in the resurrection remains firm. And he states their reasoning as an argument rather than a sneer, that they set the regular course of nature in opposition to the promise of God, concluding from the world's long continuance that it would be perpetual.
5:
The answer to the scoff is a single fact, and Calvin makes it a single argument: the world once perished by a deluge of waters, when yet it consisted of waters, and since that history was well known, those who infer the perpetuity of the world from its present state designedly close their eyes. From this he draws the conclusion he wants: the power of nature is not sufficient to sustain the world, which contains the very element of its own ruin whenever it may please God to destroy it, for the world stands through no other power than God's word, and inferior causes derive their power from him and produce different effects as they are directed. Through water the world stood, but water could have done nothing of itself; and as soon as it pleased God to destroy the earth, the same water obeyed in becoming a ruinous inundation. So they err who stop at naked elements as though there were perpetuity in them, and the petulance of those is refuted who arm themselves with physical reasons to fight against God. Barnes puts the argument as a reply to an objection: those who urged that the laws of nature were stable needed only to be shown a case in which, the same objections being available, the thing had actually happened; there was in itself as much improbability in a destruction by water as by fire, so the objection has no real force.

The difficulty is that the words describing the old world are obscure, and they say so. Clarke sets down the Greek and three rival translations before venturing his own, and then argues the question physically: it was the opinion of the remotest antiquity that the earth was formed out of a primitive moisture, and one philosopher taught pointedly that all things derive their existence from water, which very nearly expresses the apostle's sentiment in his own terms. He supports the Mosaic account from the shape of the globe, since the earth is not round but flattened at the poles and raised at the equator, the figure any soft body would assume if whirled rapidly about a centre, the equatorial diameter being greater by about twenty-five miles. Ellicott works on the words instead: the margin is nearer the truth with consisting for standing, the notion being coherence and order as against chaos, and out of water indicates the material the earth was made of, not that out of which it rose like an island. Wesley offers a physical guess of his own, that perhaps the interior globe of earth was fixed in the midst of the great deep, the exterior shell standing out of the water and covering it.

What the whereby refers to divides them further. Ellicott lists four possibilities and prefers the heavens and the earth, since both contributed to the deluge when the fountains of the great deep were broken up and the windows of heaven opened; Wesley takes it the same way. Barnes canvasses the same options and prefers the water, since the apostle had the waters of the Mosaic account prominently in his eye, and the antecedent of a pronoun is often what was in the writer's mind rather than the word he had used. Calvin meets a different objection, that the world is said to have perished though the heaven was mentioned too, and answers that the heaven was then also submerged, meaning the region of the air which stood open between the two waters, the division made at the creation being then confounded. On the present world all agree with Clarke's summary, that it is treasured up in God's storehouse to be destroyed not by water but by fire, and with Calvin's reason for expecting it, that the reason for the fire is the same as that for the water.
8:
The saying about the day and the thousand years they treat as a statement about God rather than about arithmetic. Henry says that though in the account of men there is a great difference between a day and a year, and a vast deal more between one day and a thousand years, in the account of God, who inhabits an eternity in which there is no succession, there is none, all things past and present and future being ever before him; so that the delay of a thousand years cannot be so much to him as deferring anything for an hour is to us. He makes the point urgent by turning it round: if men have no belief of the eternal God they will be apt to think him such a one as themselves. Calvin puts the same as a discipline of the eyes: waiting seems long because we fix them on the shortness of the present life and increase our weariness by computing days and hours and minutes, whereas when the eternity of God's kingdom comes into our minds many ages vanish like so many moments. The day of resurrection depends not on the present flow of time but on the hidden purpose of God, and men wish to anticipate him because they measure time by the judgment of their own flesh and are so impatient that celerity itself is delay to them. Wesley distributes the saying over four attributes — eternity, knowledge, power and longsuffering — and reads each half separately: in one day he can do the work of a thousand years, therefore he is not slow; and no delay is long to him, therefore he is longsuffering, giving us space for repentance without any inconvenience to himself.

On where the saying comes from they differ. Clarke takes it for a quotation from the Psalm and adds a pagan parallel, that a thousand or ten thousand years are but an indefinite point, or rather the smallest part of one, compared with eternity. Ellicott denies the identification: the first half is quite original and has no equivalent in the Psalm, the second only partially parallel, so we cannot be sure the apostle had the passage in mind, though it is probable enough. He then traces the saying in its other form through the second-century writers, in a martyr's dialogue, in an epistle of Barnabas, twice in one second-century father and once each in two others, noting that in no case is the context similar, and suggesting it may have been a favourite with those who held millenarian views.

The longsuffering then draws the sharpest division in the chapter, and both sides know what is at stake. Clarke takes the verse as decisive against decree: it is not slackness nor want of due displeasure at sin that makes God prolong the respite of ungodly men but his unwillingness that any should perish, and consequently he has never devised nor decreed the damnation of any man, nor made it impossible for any soul to be saved. Calvin raises the objection himself — if God wishes none to perish, why do so many perish? — and answers by a distinction: no mention is made here of the hidden purpose of God, according to which the reprobate are doomed to their own ruin, but only of his will as made known in the gospel, where he stretches forth his hand without difference to all, but lays hold only of those whom he chose before the foundation of the world. Gill narrows the promise instead, taking it of the coming to take vengeance on the Jewish nation, delayed that the elect among them might be gathered in. Ellicott reports the reading towards you rather than us-ward as beyond doubt, and notes how natural it is that Peter should not include himself, writing mainly to Gentile Christians toward whom this longsuffering had been conspicuous.
10:
Whether the manner of the burning should be investigated at all is the real division here, and Calvin settles it before the others begin. What follows respecting the burning of heaven and earth, he says, requires no long explanation, for it was not the apostle's purpose to speak refinedly of fire and storm, but only to introduce the exhortation he immediately adds, that we ought to strive after newness of life; and he reasons that as heaven and earth are to be purged by fire, the renovation of men is much more necessary. Those interpreters are mischievous who consume much labour on refined speculations when the apostle applies his doctrine to godly exhortation. Clarke and Wesley do exactly what he forbids, and at length. Clarke, taking the heavens for the atmosphere in which the terrestrial vapours are lodged, sets out the composition of water by weight and volume, notes that passing electric sparks through the two gases produces water and passing a spark through water decomposes it again, and concludes that the noise of applying fire to so immense a quantity of aqueous particles must be terrible in the extreme. He offers a demonstration: put a drop of water on an anvil, lay red-hot iron over it and strike the iron with a hammer, and the report will be as loud as a musket. Wesley asks whether God has not already provided for the event and lists three provisions — the stores of subterranean fire that so often burst out at burning mountains; the ethereal or electrical fire diffused through the globe, which would dissolve the frame of nature if the secret chain that binds it were loosed; and comets, one of which, returning from the sun heated, as a great man computes, two thousand times hotter than a red-hot cannon ball, would destroy all vegetables and animals long before contact.

What the elements are is disputed on narrower grounds. Wesley takes them for the sun, moon and stars rather than the four commonly so called, since air and water cannot melt and the earth is mentioned immediately after. Ellicott reaches the same possibility by a longer road: the difficulty of supposing fire destroyed by fire seems to exclude the four, and taking the two remaining ones is not satisfactory, so probably the various forms of matter are meant without specifying them; but since an early apologist calls the sun and moon and stars heavenly elements, and predictions of the last day speak of signs in them, the heavenly bodies may be intended, all the more since they follow immediately on the mention of the heavens. He passes on a commentator's ingenuity, connecting this with the word's root meaning of letters of the alphabet, for stars in the heaven are as letters on a scroll. Robertson gives the derivation from a word meaning a row and notes the sense in Plato.

The last clause is a textual difficulty, and two of them say so. Ellicott lays out the readings — that the works shall vanish away, shall be burned up, or shall be found, the last most strongly attested and rejected by some editors as yielding no sense — and rescues it by punctuation, placing a colon after the earth and making what follows a question: shall the works that are therein be found? He adds that happily nothing of importance turns on it, since all the variations amount practically to the same thing. Robertson lists the same witnesses more briefly and concludes that the text seems corrupt. On the suddenness they are together, and Ellicott makes an argument of it: the thief, the passing away of the heavens and the reservation for fire are three reminiscences in this chapter of one discourse of Christ which only Peter and three others seem to have heard, and this may fairly be added to the evidence for the letter's authenticity.
11:
The inference from the burning is agreed; what divides them is how the sentence runs and what the dissolving leaves behind. Clarke reports that some put the note of interrogation after what manner of persons ought ye to be, joining what follows to the next verse; Ellicott refuses it, calling the words not a question so much as an exclamation, and says that to break the sentence there would be stiff and frigid, very unlike the fervour of this epistle. On the dissolution Clarke is confident that nothing is lost: all these things will be separated and decomposed but none destroyed, and being the original matter out of which the globe was formed they may enter again into a new system, which is why the apostle goes on to speak of new heavens and a new earth. Calvin says the same in a sentence, that the elements of the world are to be consumed only that they may be renovated, their substance still remaining the same. Barnes draws the practical conclusion, that habitual contemplation of the truth that all we see is soon to pass away would make us serious, repress ambition, keep us from accumulating what must so soon be destroyed, and prompt us to lay up our treasures in heaven.

On the plurals of the eleventh verse Calvin and Ellicott make the same observation independently. Ellicott renders literally, in holy behaviours and godlinesses, and says the plurals indicate a variety of acts and occur here only. Calvin draws the moral from them, that every part of the conduct should be holy and every part of godliness attended to, so that we are not to be holy in part or pious in part but to attend to every branch of duty toward man and every branch of duty toward God. He states the argument that carries it: heaven and earth shall pass away for our sakes, and their corruptions be purged by fire though as creatures of God they are pure — what then ought to be done by us, who are full of so many pollutions? Wesley uses the same verse to settle the extent of the destruction: all these things means the universe, the stars were made on the fourth day and will be dissolved together with the earth, and they are deceived who restrain either the history of the creation or this description of the destruction to the earth and the lower heavens, imagining the stars more ancient than the earth and likely to survive it.

Whether the day can be hastened at all is the last question, and the answers are of different kinds. Clarke holds that the word translated hasting unto should be rendered earnestly desiring, or wishing for, which is a frequent meaning in the best Greek writers. Barnes takes it much the same way, of a mind anxiously desirous that the thing should occur and would accelerate it if it could, since the true Christian does not dread that day but looks to it as the period of his redemption. Ellicott prefers the margin, hasting the coming, and means it literally: Christ's coming is hastened by holy lives, by making the gospel known to all nations so as to accomplish the number of the elect, and by praying that his kingdom come. He adds that the thought is singularly parallel to Peter's own speech in Solomon's Porch, and that being striking and unusual it may fairly be admitted as a note of genuineness. Clarke closes with the pagan witnesses, quoting a Latin poet on the time when sea and land and the palace of heaven shall burn, and reporting that the Stoics held the world would catch fire when the moisture of the earth was consumed, as did the Epicureans. And he notices what nobody thought: none ever fancied that it would be destroyed by water, the tradition being against it.
13:
All four send the promise back to the same two places in Isaiah, where God declares that he creates a new heaven and a new earth, that the former shall not be remembered nor come into mind, and that what he makes shall remain before him. Ellicott corrects the emphasis of the English, which he says falls wrongly on we and should fall on new, and then distinguishes the two Greek words for new: one looks forward, young as opposed to aged, the other looks back, fresh as opposed to worn out, and it is the latter that stands here. He also notes that looking for is repeated three times in three verses, and reads the clause about righteousness as a claim about residence — righteousness has its home there and is not a wanderer and changeful guest as on earth, from which he draws the duty, that by righteousness we must make ourselves worthy of entering. Robertson makes the same point flatly, that righteousness is certainly not at home in this present world, in individuals, families, or nations.

What the new world will be they are more careful about. Barnes says at once that many of the questions naturally asked cannot easily be answered, and that whether this globe, once purified by fire, will be furnished again for the redeemed is impossible to settle with certainty. He then sets out three senses any of which the word would bear. One is a creation out of nothing once this frame is gone, which is possible though nowhere revealed. Another is that a man should live after death upon some other of the worlds now existing, where everything would be strange to him: let him be carried to the planet Saturn, with its wonderful ring and its seven moons, and every aspect of sky and dwelling-place would be so. The third is that this globe should be renovated and fitted up for mankind once the universal conflagration is over. Clarke takes the third without hesitation: the present globe, though destined to be burned up, will not perish but be renewed and refined, purged of every moral and natural imperfection, and made the endless dwelling of blessed spirits; and he adds that it is more reasonable and philosophical to conclude that it shall be refined and restored than annihilated.

Both of them then guard the same flank, and for the same reason. Clarke insists that this condition belongs wholly after the day of judgment, on which the apostle is very express, and says plainly that it has nothing to do with what some call the millennium, since that would fall while the present order still stood. Barnes argues from the order of the chapter: sky and land are first kept in store against the day of judgment, that day then comes suddenly and the elements melt, and only afterwards are we told what to expect. Nothing is said of a personal reign of Christ, nothing of saints raised to live with him below, nothing of any refurnishing before the assize. He puts the weight on the silence: this is one of the very few places in the New Testament where the manner of the world's closing is described, and if the writer had looked for such a reign it cannot be explained why the subject should have been passed over here in total silence.
14:
The exhortation is drawn from the hope, and Calvin says why the inference holds: hope is living and efficacious, so it cannot but attract us to itself, and he who waits for a renewed heaven must begin with renewal in himself, while they who cleave to their own filth think nothing of God's kingdom and have no taste for anything but this corrupt world. He fastens on the phrase found by him, since while the world engrosses the minds of others we must cast our eyes on the Lord, and that is real integrity which is approved by his judgment rather than that which gains the praise of men. He raises the obvious difficulty, how anyone can be found blameless when we all labour under so many deficiencies, and answers that the apostle points out the mark all the faithful are to aim at, though they cannot reach it until, having put off the flesh, they are wholly united to Christ. On the words in peace he prefers a quiet conscience founded on hope and patient waiting to peace with God, since it is because so few attend to the judgment of Christ that men are carried headlong by their lusts and are at the same time disquieted. Ellicott corrects the construction, since found of him means rather in his sight, and notes that spotless and blameless coincides with the first epistle and contrasts with the false teachers, who were called spots and blemishes; he doubts that in peace has any special reference, taking it to express at once the condition and the consequence of being spotless.

Whether the Lord here is the Father or Christ is disputed, and Ellicott weighs it carefully. In one verse of this chapter the Lord certainly means God, in another our Lord is expressly Jesus Christ, and the two between are disputable; but the presence of our here inclines the balance toward the latter, and had God been meant it would have sufficed to say his longsuffering. If that is right, then throughout this weighty passage the Lord Jesus is invested with the full attributes of Deity. Robertson takes the same view more briefly, and Clarke passes on an argument for citing Paul here at all, that the persons to whom these epistles were sent were for the most part Paul's own converts, and that he had written to several of those churches things implying that God's forbearance with sinners is intended for their salvation.

The mention of Paul then produces the chapter's sharpest disagreement about the letter itself. Ellicott makes the phrase our beloved brother Paul a decided note of genuineness, since it implies a familiarity and equality in marked contrast to the way the sub-apostolic writers speak of him — one calls him the blessed Paul the Apostle, another the sanctified, the martyred, worthily called blessed, another the blessed and glorious Paul, another simply the Apostle or the divine Apostle — and an imitator in the second century would scarcely have attained to such freedom. Robertson hears both warmth and reserve in it, quoting the judgment that Peter speaks of Paul with affection and respect yet maintains the right to criticise. Calvin, examining all things more narrowly, reaches the opposite conclusion: it seems to him more probable that this epistle was composed by another according to what Peter communicated than that Peter wrote it himself, for Peter would never have spoken thus; and it is enough for him that we have here a witness of Peter's doctrine and goodwill who brought forward nothing contrary to what he would have said. He also supplies the motive for naming Paul, that unprincipled men went about to discredit Paul by pretending he did not agree with the other apostles, so it was necessary to take away the occasion for such a calumny.
16:
Which letter of Paul's is meant, and where the difficulty lies, are the two questions. Calvin's discussion settles on Hebrews, on the ground that the subjects referred to are those of the preceding verses — the day of judgment, the future state and the need to be ready for it — and that the promise of a renewed heaven and earth answers exactly to the better and heavenly country of that epistle, whose warnings coincide with the exhortation given here. Ellicott points instead to the second letter to the Thessalonians, whose difficulties bristle about the very point in question, and which scoffers could turn to account by arguing that the man of sin had not yet appeared; he reports that many refer the words rather to justification by faith, wrested to mean faith without works, and notes that Paul saw his own teaching on Christian liberty to be liable to great abuse and already abused. On the text Clarke sets out the alternative: with the common reading the hard things are the matters spoken of, but on the reading of several manuscripts and versions the difficulties are in all the epistles — and indeed, he asks, in what ancient writings are there not difficulties?

What the word wrest means they agree about, and it is a violent word. Ellicott says it is literally to torture by the rack, and hence to strain or distort; Clarke gives the same, to overstretch and dislocate the limbs, and says the persons meant are those who proceed by no fair plan of interpretation but force unnatural and sophistical meanings on the word of God. Ellicott distinguishes the unlearned here from the word so translated elsewhere, this one meaning without ordinary instruction rather than without special study, and observes that ignorance naturally produces instability, those who have no clear principles of doctrine falling easy victims to seduction. Both press that the destruction is the men's own doing: it is their own, emphatically so in the Greek, and the writers of Scripture are not to blame.

Then all four turn the verse against the use commonly made of it, and none of them is gentle. Calvin states the principle: we are not forbidden to read Paul's epistles because they contain things hard to be understood, but rather they are commended to us, provided we bring a calm and teachable mind; the apostle condemns men who are trifling and volatile, and though the same is commonly done to all Scripture, he does not conclude that we are not to read it, but that the vices which prevent improvement ought to be corrected. He allows the obscurity and explains it, that it is nothing to wonder at in the mysteries of Christ's kingdom, since many are blind who stumble at midday. Ellicott is exact: the passage gives no countenance to the doctrine that all Scripture is hard and therefore not to be read by the people, since all that is said is that some Scripture is hard and that bad men make a bad use of the fact; and the inference drawn is not do not read, nor even pass over what seems hard, but be on your guard against interpretations contrary to the spirit of the gospel. Clarke argues it at length and closes with a challenge, that a single instance cannot be adduced of any soul perverted or destroyed by reading the Bible, and that the insinuation is blasphemous. Wesley says it in one line: that some use the Scriptures ill is no reason why others should not use them at all. On the other scriptures Wesley and Ellicott part company, the one taking the phrase to prove that Paul's writings were by then part of Scripture, the other holding that the Old Testament can hardly be meant and that Christian writings of some kind are intended, perhaps including some that are not canonical.
17:
The warning to beware raises an old difficulty, and Calvin meets it directly. It seems, he says, that we stand on slippery ground and that the certainty of our salvation hangs as it were on a thread, since the faithful are told to take heed lest they fall from their own steadfastness; what then will become of us if we are exposed to the danger of falling? His answer is that such exhortations are by no means intended to shake the firmness of that faith which rests on God, but to correct the sloth of our flesh: as long as we are in the flesh our tardiness must be roused, and it is fitly roused by having our weakness and the dangers around us set before our eyes, without the confidence which rests on God's promises being shaken. Robertson makes the sterner point, that being forewarned they are without excuse for misunderstanding either Peter or Paul. Ellicott notices where the word for being carried away is used elsewhere and finds it strange: of its three places in the New Testament, one is the account of Barnabas being carried away with the dissimulation of Peter himself. He observes too that the word for steadfastness occurs nowhere else, and that this verse and the last both refer back to the opening, so that the coherence between beginning and ending is complete.

From this Ellicott builds an argument about the order of two letters: the absence of any directions as to how these evil men and their victims are to be treated, which the epistle of Jude gives rather elaborately, tells for this letter being earlier, since when evil men begin to arise the first impulse is to avoid them, whereas when they have established themselves people begin to consider how to deal with the seducers and win back the seduced. He argues the same way from the ending, which is abrupt and has no greetings: this is so unlike the first epistle and apostolic letters generally that so accomplished an imitator would scarcely have omitted them, doubly natural as they would be in one personating an apostle near the end of his life, writing to congregations he would never address again. Assume the apostle himself is writing, and the disappointment is explained: his heart is too full of the dangers threatening the whole community to think of himself.

On growing in grace Clarke and Wesley both argue from the body, and agree even in the warning. Clarke says the life of a Christian is a growth, since he is at first born of God and a little child, becomes a young man and a father in Christ, and every father was once an infant; in the order of nature the infant that does not grow daily is sickly and soon dies, and so in grace; many boast of their conversion who were never more than babes and have long since lost even that. Wesley says there may be for a time grace without growth, as there may be natural life without growth, but such sickly life will end in death and every day draw nigher to it; the strength of a Christian depends on what his soul feeds on, and sin of every kind starves it. On the doxology Calvin and Ellicott make the same doctrinal point from different evidence. Calvin calls it a remarkable passage to prove the divinity of Christ, since what is said cannot belong to any but God alone, and notes that the word now is designed so that we may not rob Christ of his glory during our warfare here. Ellicott says there can be no doubt that here homage is paid to Jesus Christ as true God, and suggests this may be the earliest example of that hymn to Christ as God which a Roman governor reported to his emperor that the Christians sang before daybreak.
